unmapped_findings: For the high-temperature rolling zone (R850/R950) the phase hardness mismatch follows martensite (5.98–6.50 GPa) > DIF (2.84–2.98 GPa) > δ-ferrite (2.64–2.77 GPa), with a maximum hardness difference reaching 3.86 GPa.

Impact absorption energy of the test steel in the high-temperature rolling zone decreases significantly to <10 J; R950 (4.6 ± 0.2 J) fails by typical brittle fracture with cracks propagating straight through the carbide-free honeycomb structure with no blunting or deflection.

R950 belongs to the high-temperature rolling zone where carbides dissolve completely and the structure transforms into a duplex δ-ferrite lamellae + honeycomb martensite lamellae structure containing equiaxed DIF grains that grow with increasing rolling temperature.

Hardness of each phase in the high-temperature rolling zone exhibits a gradient distribution; the large hardness difference between phases causes stress concentration at phase boundaries, which become preferential sites for crack initiation.

In the R950 condition the equiaxed DIF grains originate from two mechanisms: dynamic recrystallization (new grains with increased HAGB and GOS≤2° fractions and decreased KAM/dislocation density) and deformation-induced ferrite transformation (DIFT) during hot rolling, with DIF having submicron size and higher hardness than recrystallized ferrite.

Abstract-level statement for the high-temperature rolling zone: impact energy less than 7 J at room temperature with elongation less than 9 %, and a monotonically decreasing θ-curve due to phase hardness mismatch (martensite/ferrite hardness difference >3.3 GPa).
